The missing solution to the unsatisfying situation of unmotivated definitions of combinatorial generating functions (like the Catalan or Fibonacci sequence and others throughout Mathlib) is a CombinatorialClass (described in [1][2]), containing objects of size n the number of which generate the sequence. Since this is so well defined in the literature, I thought we should have it. So, with the help of Opus, these 170 lines resulted: https://github.com/rwst/mathlib4/blob/comb01/Mathlib/Combinatorics/Enumerative/GeneratingFunction.lean It's trivial enough that even I can see it's a faithful formalization.

Of course SEQ and other operators are missing (see TODO). I think @Yaël Dillies had a similar project? Do I get your support for the PR?

What's already possible with this is, e.g to derive the functional equation of the Fibonacci OGF from a description of square/domino tilings of the $n$-strip:

public import Mathlib.Combinatorics.Enumerative.GeneratingFunction
public import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Fib.Basic
public import Mathlib.Data.Set.Finite.List

open PowerSeries CombinatorialClass
namespace TilingExample

/-- The atomic class with a single object of size `k`. -/
def atom (k : ℕ) : CombinatorialClass where
  carrier := Unit
  size _ := k
  finite_fiber _ := Finite.of_injective Subtype.val Subtype.val_injective

theorem atom_card (k m : ℕ) : (atom k).card m = if m = k then 1 else 0 := by
  have hc : (atom k).card m = Nat.card {_u : Unit // k = m} := rfl
  rw [hc]
  by_cases h : m = k
  · subst h
    rw [if_pos rfl, Nat.card_congr (Equiv.subtypeUnivEquiv fun _ : Unit => rfl)]
    exact Nat.card_unique
  · rw [if_neg h]
    haveI : IsEmpty {_u : Unit // k = m} := ⟨fun x => h x.2.symm⟩
    exact Nat.card_of_isEmpty

/-- The OGF of the size-`k` atom is `Xᵏ`. -/
theorem atom_ogf (k : ℕ) : (atom k).ogf = (X : PowerSeries ℕ) ^ k := by
  ext m
  rw [coeff_ogf, atom_card, coeff_X_pow]

/-! ### Tiles and tilings -/

/-- A single tile: a square (size 1) or a domino (size 2). -/
def tile : CombinatorialClass := (atom 1).sum (atom 2)

instance : Finite tile.carrier := inferInstanceAs (Finite (Unit ⊕ Unit))

/-- `Tile = square ⊕ domino`, so `tile.ogf = X + X²`. -/
theorem tile_ogf : tile.ogf = (X : PowerSeries ℕ) + X ^ 2 := by
  rw [tile, ogf_sum, atom_ogf, atom_ogf, pow_one]

/-- Size of a tiling: total length covered. -/
def tsize (l : List tile.carrier) : ℕ := (l.map tile.size).sum

@[simp] theorem tsize_nil : tsize [] = 0 := rfl

@[simp] theorem tsize_cons (t : tile.carrier) (l : List tile.carrier) :
    tsize (t :: l) = tile.size t + tsize l := rfl

theorem one_le_tile_size (t : tile.carrier) : 1 ≤ tile.size t := by
  rcases t with _ | _ <;> simp [tile, CombinatorialClass.sum, atom]

theorem length_le_tsize (l : List tile.carrier) : l.length ≤ tsize l := by
  induction l with
  | nil => simp
  | cons t l ih =>
      simp only [List.length_cons, tsize_cons]
      have := one_le_tile_size t
      omega

/-- The class of tilings: lists of tiles, sized by total length covered. -/
def tiling : CombinatorialClass where
  carrier := List tile.carrier
  size := tsize
  finite_fiber n := by
    have hfin : {l : List tile.carrier | tsize l = n}.Finite :=
      (List.finite_length_le tile.carrier n).subset fun l hl =>
        le_of_le_of_eq (length_le_tsize l) hl
    exact hfin.to_subtype

/-- The cons decomposition `Tiling ≅ 1 ⊕ (Tile × Tiling)`, as a bijection. -/
def tilingDecomp : List tile.carrier ≃ (Unit ⊕ tile.carrier × List tile.carrier) where
  toFun
    | [] => Sum.inl ()
    | t :: l => Sum.inr (t, l)
  invFun
    | Sum.inl _ => []
    | Sum.inr (t, l) => t :: l
  left_inv := by rintro (_ | ⟨t, l⟩) <;> rfl
  right_inv := by rintro (⟨⟩ | ⟨t, l⟩) <;> rfl

/-- **The derived functional equation of the Fibonacci OGF.** -/
theorem tiling_ogf : tiling.ogf = 1 + (X + X ^ 2) * tiling.ogf := by
  have hcongr : tiling.ogf = ((atom 0).sum (tile.prod tiling)).ogf :=
    ogf_congr (𝒜 := tiling) (ℬ := (atom 0).sum (tile.prod tiling))
      tilingDecomp (by rintro (_ | ⟨t, l⟩) <;> rfl)
  nth_rewrite 1 [hcongr]
  rw [ogf_sum, ogf_prod, atom_ogf, pow_zero, tile_ogf]

* 1 [P. Flajolet and R. Sedgewick, *Analytic Combinatorics*][flajolet2009]
* 2 [M. Bona, *Handbook of Enumerative Combinatorics*][Bona2015]

Or a second example, the connection between binary trees and the Catalan sequence (without the functional eq.):

public import Mathlib.Combinatorics.Enumerative.GeneratingFunction
public import Mathlib.Combinatorics.Enumerative.Catalan.Tree
public import Mathlib.RingTheory.PowerSeries.Catalan

open Finset PowerSeries CombinatorialClass Tree

/-- The trees with exactly `n` internal nodes are the elements of the finset
`treesOfNumNodesEq n`. -/
def treeFiberEquiv (n : ℕ) :
    {t : Tree Unit // t.numNodes = n} ≃ treesOfNumNodesEq n :=
  Equiv.subtypeEquivRight fun _ => mem_treesOfNumNodesEq.symm

/-- Binary trees (`Tree Unit`), sized by their number of internal nodes, as a
combinatorial class. -/
def binaryTree : CombinatorialClass where
  carrier := Tree Unit
  size := Tree.numNodes
  finite_fiber n := Finite.of_equiv _ (treeFiberEquiv n).symm

/-- The number of size-`n` binary trees is `catalan n` — reusing Mathlib's existing
`treesOfNumNodesEq_card_eq_catalan`. -/
theorem binaryTree_card (n : ℕ) : binaryTree.card n = catalan n :=
  (Nat.card_congr (treeFiberEquiv n)).trans <|
    Nat.card_eq_fintype_card.trans <|
      (Fintype.card_coe _).trans (treesOfNumNodesEq_card_eq_catalan n)

theorem binaryTree_ogf : binaryTree.ogf = catalanSeries := by
  ext n
  rw [coeff_ogf, binaryTree_card, catalanSeries_coeff]

Coming from enumerative combinatorics myself, I have also been thinking about how to write a definition for a combinatorial class in Lean. The natural definition of an ordinary (or exponential) generating function is fine, but my feeling is that one would like to also have multivariate generating functions.

In my experience, most instances can be defined as power series in one variable, with coefficients in rings of (possibly multivariate) polynomials, corresponding to additional parameters for the GF (which are bounded for given "size", corresponding to the main variable). But there are also cases where one would need "true" multivariate power series (when the second parameter is unbounded for given "size"). The common factor is that, in all cases, the GF is the sum over all elements of the class of some weight, which is normally a monomial (with coefficient not necessarily 1, for EGF).

I'm not enough of an expert in library design to decide what the "right" design would be (or even if one would be a good idea).

Yes, Flajolet-Sedgewick develop into multivariate GF later in the book, and there is a bunch more dedicated works (Pemantle, Wilson, and Melczer; Goulden and Jackson; ...). The framework here is only a start.

The GFs in analytic combinatorics are typically seen as analytic functions, so power series are not necessarily the right tool for this part - unless I am misunderstanding what Mathlib knows, evaluation of power series does not cover radius of convergence questions.

But, I am very interested in seeing where this goes!
Is the Pascal Triangle also subject to this topic?

Philippe Duchon said:

The GFs in analytic combinatorics are typically seen as analytic functions, so power series are not necessarily the right tool for this part - unless I am misunderstanding what Mathlib knows, evaluation of power series does not cover radius of convergence questions.

The power series here are formal, convergence questions don't apply.

Ian Allen said:

Is the Pascal Triangle also subject to this topic?

GFs for the Pascal triangle are the most elementary of multivariate GFs: 1/(1-y-xy) (OGF), exp(x+x*y) (EGF). The combinatorial objects associated could be

  • lattice paths from (0,0) to (n,k) using steps (1,0) and (1,1)
  • coefficients in expansion of (1+x)^n
  • number of ways of placing k indistinguishable balls into n boxes
    (taken from https://oeis.org/A007318 where there is much more)

Philippe Duchon said:

The GFs in analytic combinatorics are typically seen as analytic functions, so power series are not necessarily the right tool for this part - unless I am misunderstanding what Mathlib knows, evaluation of power series does not cover radius of convergence questions.

It is easy to find the closed form of the power series coefficients of a rational GF by partial fraction decomposition. Other GF types have other closed forms, too. These would be used in analysis, I guess.

Philippe Duchon said:

The common factor is that, in all cases, the GF is the sum over all elements of the class of some weight, which is normally a monomial (with coefficient not necessarily 1, for EGF).

It seems the framework can be extended orthogonally to have a weight axis. It would be good design to include this from the start, and it naturally leads to multivariate GFs.

You need to use some form of topology (possibly infinite sums) if you want a theorem that the GF is the sum of weights of elements of the combinatorial class. But the topology is a simple one (simple convergence from the discrete topology), and Mathlib knows about it.

this looks like a nice development to me — one possible counter or complimentary proposal could be a formalisation of species of structures, that is, an assignment of (finite) types to (finite) types which is functorial in bijections (this wouldn't have to be defined use the category theory library imo). i'd believe it if someone told me this wasn't worth the DTT (or otherwise) pain but it's appealing to me from a couple of perspectives

  • there are natural combinatorial classes which don't live in the same type, eg permutations of a finite set
  • there are natural operations which could be stated nicely in this language, for instance if a species F has EGF f then the species α ↦ F (Option α) has EGF f'
  • composition of EGFs corresponds exactly to compositions of the functors (EDIT this is not true at all, the composition of EGFs corresponds to a more complicated operation)

full disclosure i am not a combinatorialist — as a dilettante i am interested in seeing bone fide enumerative combinatorics in mathlib & i am more than happy to defer to the opinions of people who know better :))
Thanks. I can see now that species would be the generalization (after the EGF/labelled classes addition). Let me submit this PR first. It's already bigger than planned.

I let Opus implement one last design change: remove structures and do a typeclass approach. The Catalan example now reduces to

public import Mathlib.Combinatorics.Enumerative.GeneratingFunction
public import Mathlib.Combinatorics.Enumerative.Catalan.Tree
public import Mathlib.RingTheory.PowerSeries.Catalan

open Finset PowerSeries Combinatorics Tree

def treeFiberEquiv (n : ℕ) :
    {t : Tree Unit // t.numNodes = n} ≃ treesOfNumNodesEq n :=
  Equiv.subtypeEquivRight fun _ => mem_treesOfNumNodesEq.symm

instance : FiniteSizeFibers (Tree.numNodes : Tree Unit → ℕ) :=
  ⟨fun n => Finite.of_equiv _ (treeFiberEquiv n).symm⟩

theorem binaryTree_card (n : ℕ) :
    Nat.card {t : Tree Unit // t.numNodes = n} = catalan n :=
  (Nat.card_congr (treeFiberEquiv n)).trans <|
    Nat.card_eq_fintype_card.trans <|
      (Fintype.card_coe _).trans (treesOfNumNodesEq_card_eq_catalan n)

theorem binaryTree_ogf : ogf (Tree.numNodes : Tree Unit → ℕ) = catalanSeries := by
  ext n
  rw [coeff_ogf, binaryTree_card, catalanSeries_coeff]

Hello Philippe! The functor which appears at an early paragraph of Wikipedia's page on species should really not worry you. To give an example, take the species of trees. Then, for any set SSS, you have the set T(S)\mathcal T(S)T(S) of trees with vertices SSS. This is the functor. What makes it a functor is that if you have a bijection f ⁣:S→S′f\colon S\to S'f:S→S′, you can transform any tree with vertices SSS to a tree with vertices S′S'S′, simply by relabelling. This is a map T(f) ⁣:T(S)→T(S′)\mathcal T(f)\colon \mathcal T(S)\to\mathcal T(S')T(f):T(S)→T(S′), which is clearly bijective because the map in the other direction is $$\mathcal T(f^{-1})$. And this relabelling process satisfies T(idS)=idT(S)\mathcal T(\mathrm{id}_S)=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal T(S)}T(idS​)=idT(S)​ and T(f∘g)=T(f)∘T(g)\mathcal T(f \circ g)=\mathcal T(f)\circ \mathcal T(g)T(f∘g)=T(f)∘T(g), more or less obviously. There's really not much more.

Hi Philippe! Antoine's explanation exactly captures the content of the definition "a species is a functor ...". For some extra context, the reason I like the functorial language is that it emphasises that a species — say the collection of permutations of some set — is more than the function which comes from the counting sequence (n ↦ n! in that case), it is a concrete construction on a (finite) type. From that perspective, the reason the species (specieses?) of orderings Fin (card α) → α and permutations Equiv.Perm α are not isomorphic is that the conversion between them requires fixing an ordering on α at the beginning, which you might not have for generic α (leaving aside the subtleties of what I mean by "finite" in type theory). The statement that "a species is a functor from ..." is (to my mind) a way of formalising the fact that the construction of the combinatorial object you're interested in doesn't depend on the specific finite set (type, labelling) you pick — in the case of permutations vs lists, the usual bijection between them relies on starting with the finite set {1, 2, ..., n}, is as such is not "natural" in a precise sense.

I am interested in formalizing this as well, from a point of view of analytic combinatorics (e.g. Flajolet & Sedgewick). My hope would be to leverage the mechanism from Lean's kernel in order to do most of the heavy lifting. Here are some thoughts - apologies for any misunderstanding I may have about how Lean works, I am currently halfway through Mathematics in Lean.

Main idea: inductive types reflect quite closely how many combinatorial objects are defined or decomposed. They also have a sizeOf function that ensures they are "finite" (which might need to get overridden for specific examples). Once we have a specification of a combinatorial class as an inductive type, it seems like one could automate away a lot of tasks, including

  • showing that the set of objects of this type with a given size is finite and providing a procedure to compute it,
  • defining the generating function and providing a procedure to compute the first terms,
  • showing that the radius of convergence of the generating function is non-zero,
  • obtaining a set of equations characterizing the generating function...

Perhaps one could even encode all this in an instance and use the typeclass inference mechanism?

You can certainly do something like this, but my understanding is then you will have to define an inductive type for each individual combinatorial class. Also, I don't think there is a simple way to define which functions from an inductive type will be valid "size" functions - you can write an axiomatic condition that the preimage of each singleton is finite or whatever, but then you are not ensuring that the size definition follows the inductive definition, in an additive fashion - a condition that is satisfied by the vast majority of families of combinatorial objects that appear in Flajolet & Sedgewick.

A natural approximation would be to have the size of an object be the number of constructor invocations in its definition, but if there is a systematic way of having this, I don't know how - also, you'd want to restrict the constructions in inductive types.

@Philippe Duchon Thank you for your input! I don't know enough Mathlib to think about how to handle a certain number of considerations - like multivariate generating functions, or determining which functions are valid size functions. I will keep that in mind as I progress through Mathematics in Lean and ultimately take a look at the section on well-founded recursion in the Lean Language Reference.

To address your first remark: with this approach, combinatorial classes wouldn't be synonymous with inductive types, but from (m)any inductive type one could derive a combinatorial class. Providing an inductive construction would then make certain things easier, but wouldn't be required.

I don't expect to be able to cover any and all cases, for the reason you pointed out concerning size functions. That's where typeclass inference could prove useful: if we create a bunch of instances for "elementary blocks", like Seq, Prod, Add, etc, it would be straightforward to conclude that any combinatorial class constructed from these is valid. For more exotic ones one would have to provide more work.

I'd love to discuss this with you (and/or any combinatorist who might be reading this) at a later point when I have a more precise idea of the situation!

One thing this thread makes me think about is review surface, not just automation.

For a combinatorial class interface, it seems useful if the abstraction compresses a claim like “these objects generate this sequence” into a small set of checkable data:

  • the object family or type;
  • the semantic size/weight;
  • finite fibers, or an explicit enumeration with a correctness theorem;
  • coefficient/cardinality theorems;
  • constructor equations, where available;
  • and eventually the dependency/axiom footprint of the generated facts.

That feels especially important if AI-assisted generation enters the workflow. The bottleneck is not only producing definitions/proofs; it is making the generated evidence reviewable. A reviewer should be able to inspect the invariant and the proof surface without reading a large generated tree.

So maybe the design goal is not just “derive generating functions automatically,” but “derive them in a way that exposes the semantic invariant and makes the resulting evidence easy to audit.”

Edit:
I got robot emojied :see_no_evil: Still learning the norms and proper tone to take in the community, but I stand by the original point. A good combinatorial-class abstraction should expose a small, inspectable proof surface, especially now that generating code and evidence candidates is now cheap.
